(p-1) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surah al-Hajj

Its purpose is to urge taqwa (God-consciousness), which raises a person from the rank of deserving judgment by justice to the rank of being worthy of the bestowal of grace, on the Day of Gathering for Judgment. The most suitable thing in it for this is the Hajj, which is evident. (In the name of Allah), whose greatness requires that everything submit (the Most Gracious), who by His mercy and justice encompasses every existing thing (the Most Merciful), who by His grace singles out whom He wills from among those of His justice.

When the surah before it ended with warning of the Great Terror, the folding up of the heavens, the coming of what they were promised, and the recompense in accordance with what they deserve, and the greatest of these is the Day of Judgment, this surah opens with a command to taqwa, which saves one from the terror of that Day. He said: ﴿O mankind﴾, i.e., those of whom it was mentioned at the beginning of that [surah] that ﴿their reckoning has drawn near for them﴾. ﴿Be mindful of your Lord﴾, i.e., beware of the punishment of the One who has bestowed upon you every kind of favour, by placing between yourselves and Him a shield of obedience.

(p-2) Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said: When the surah of al-Anbiya' was opened with His saying, ﴿The reckoning of mankind has drawn near for them﴾ [al-Anbiya': 1], and this occurred in the context of threat, and it was repeated in several places in it, such as His saying: ﴿To Us you will be returned﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 57]; ﴿I will show you My signs, so do not seek to hasten [them]﴾ [al-Anbiya': 37]; ﴿And they say, "When is this promise?"﴾ [al-Anbiya': 38]; ﴿If only those who disbelieved knew the time when they will not be able to ward off the Fire from their faces﴾ [al-Anbiya': 39]; ﴿And if a breath of the punishment of your Lord touches them﴾ [al-Anbiya': 46]; ﴿And We set up the scales of justice for the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Anbiya': 47]; ﴿And they, from the Hour, are fearful﴾ [al-Anbiya': 49]; ﴿All to Us will return﴾ [al-Anbiya': 93]; ﴿And the true promise has drawn near﴾ [al-Anbiya': 97]; ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell﴾ [al-Anbiya': 98]; ﴿The Day We will roll up the heaven like the rolling of a scroll for the records﴾ [al-Anbiya': 104]; along with what lay between these verses of threat and severe warning, to the extent that you can hardly find verses like these in warning and admonition concerning the Hour, what follows it and what precedes it, in parallels of this surah. It was concluded with the like of what it began with, and there followed what is appropriate to it of the announcement of the terror of the Hour and the greatness of its matter. So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿O mankind, be mindful of your Lord﴾ – up to His saying: ﴿But the punishment of Allah is severe﴾ [al-Hajj: 2]. Then He followed this with an extensive presentation of the proofs of the final Resurrection and the establishment of the argument: ﴿O mankind, if you are in doubt about the Resurrection﴾ [al-Hajj: 5], and the verses [that follow]. Then He said: ﴿That is because Allah is the Truth﴾ [al-Hajj: 6], i.e., this wondrous ruling is consistent and clear, [as seen in] your transformation from one state to another in the wombs and after your emergence into (p-3) the world, while you know this from yourselves; and you witness the earth in a state of stillness and death until the time water descends upon it, and then We bring it to life and bring forth kinds of plants and varieties of fruits, ﴿irrigated with one water﴾ [al-Ra'd: 4]. ﴿That is because Allah is the Truth, and that He gives life to the dead﴾ [al-Hajj: 6], just as He gave you life first and brought you out from non-existence into existence, and gave life to the earth after its death and stillness. Likewise the Hour will come without any doubt or uncertainty, and He will resurrect you for what He has promised you of your reckoning and recompense, ﴿a party in Paradise and a party in the Blaze﴾ [al-Shura: 7]. End of quotation.

When He commanded them to taqwa, He gave a reason for it, warning them, saying: ﴿Indeed, the quaking of the Hour﴾, i.e., the one about which warning was previously given in al-Anbiya', at its beginning and end and in between, meaning the severity of its agitation and its violent shaking that removes things from their places with great removal, by means of the various sounds and disturbing, continuous movements that occur in it, from the blowing into the Trumpet, the scattering of the graves, and what results from that of the wonders of the decreed matter, at the time of standing and the intensifying of crowding. This is because zalzala is the doubled form of zalla (to slip or move from its place quickly); its wording was doubled to match the doubling of its meaning. al-Baghawi said: zalzalah and zilzal: the intensity of movement in a terrifying state. End of quotation. And it is an idafah of the masdar (verbal noun) to its agent or to its object of time (the "in which" construction). ﴿Is a thing tremendous﴾, i.e., the intellects cannot comprehend its description. (p-4) Ibn Kathir said: i.e., a great matter, a grave affair, a terrible occurrence, a frightful event, and a wondrous happening. End of quotation.

This is said regarding the quaking itself; then how [will it be] with all that happens on that Day, on which there is no escape for you from being gathered to Allah, so that He may recompense you for what you did, when not the smallest speck nor the thinnest membrane will be forgotten, and not the least or the greatest will be hidden, of things before which hearts will fly up and souls cannot remain steady. So prepare yourselves and strive against your enemies from among the desires and the devils.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 22, verse 2:

Since the intended meaning of "al-Sa'ah" (the Hour) is the Resurrection and what surrounds it, it is made the container (maẓrūf) for that Day, which is from that time until the separation of the two groups into the two abodes of distance (from Allah) and felicity, of humiliation and forgiveness. So Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿On the Day you see it﴾, that is, the earthquake, or "every nursing mother" (the pronoun being implied before mention), to magnify the matter and to startle the soul. ﴿Every nursing mother will be distracted﴾, that is, will forget and be heedless, bewildered and dazed. This (tadhhalu) is the governing element (al-'āmil) of "yawma" (on the Day). It is also permissible that its governing element be the sense of the speech, meaning: you will greatly magnify that Day when you witness it, even though you now deny it. What follows is then a resumed statement (isti'nāf). By the use of "al-Sūr" (the Trumpet) he indicated the generality of its effect, due to the intensity of its greatness. So He says: ﴿every nursing mother﴾, that is, in actuality, ﴿will abandon what she has nursed﴾ of her child and others, and she is the one who died while her infant was nursing with her. Al-Baghawi said: It is said "murḍi'" (nursing) without the "ha'" (ta' marbuta) when it is intended as an attribute, like "ḥā'iḍ" (menstruating) and "ḥāmil" (pregnant); when they intend the act they add the "ha'." That is, it then indicates that she is engaged in it. ﴿And every pregnant one will drop her load﴾, that is, will abort it before completion, out of terror and fright, and she is the one who died while pregnant. And Allah knows best, for every person will be raised upon what he died upon. Al-Hasan said: The nursing mother will be distracted from her child without weaning, and the pregnant one will deliver what is in her womb without completion. End of quotation. What supports that this earthquake occurs after the resurrection is what is in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs and others: Muslim in al-Īmān, and this is its wording, and al-Bukhari, at the explanation of this verse, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him, who traced it to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: O Adam! He says: Here I am at Your service and call, and all good is in Your hands. He says: Bring forth the group for the Fire. He says: And what is the group for the Fire? He says: Of every thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine," then: "That is the time when the child grows old, and every pregnant one drops her load." The hadith... and the narrations on this are numerous, and those opposing them are weak. Also appropriate to what comes at the end of that passage is His saying: ﴿Then, behold, the eyes of those who disbelieved will stare fixedly﴾ [al-Anbiya': 97], and what follows it, that this earthquake is after the rising from the graves: ﴿On the Day We fold up the heaven﴾ [al-Anbiya': 104], ﴿When the heaven is split asunder﴾ [al-Infitar: 1], up to His saying: ﴿a soul will know what it has sent forward and what it has left behind﴾ [al-Infitar: 5]. It is possible that the intended meaning is this and what precedes it, because the Day of the Hour is long, so its relation to all of them is on an equal footing.

Since all people see the earthquake, and a person does not see drunkenness except from another, He said regarding the earthquake, ﴿you see it﴾, and regarding the drunkenness He said: ﴿and you see people as drunk﴾, that is, because of the astonishment, bewilderment and stupefaction they are in, due to what they witness of the veil of might, the authority of dominion, and the pavilion of majesty. Then He indicated that this is not in its reality by His saying, negating what might be presumed to be affirmed by the first sentence: ﴿but they are not drunk﴾, that is, from wine.

When He negated that they were drunk from wine, He affirmed what made that state necessary for them, so He said: ﴿but the punishment of Allah﴾, Possessor of might and dominion, ﴿is severe﴾. It is He who made it necessary to assume drunkenness for them, because it removed their fear from around them and its terror made their minds fly away.

**Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 22, verse 3:**

(p-٧) When the following conjunction (*ʿaṭf*) made clear that people are of two kinds, and that the implied sense is: "Then among you is he who believes and so fears God and is saved from the evil of that Day, in which wisdom required the manifestation of His greatness, so that the party of God would increase in joy and the party of Satan in grief and sorrow," he joined to it His saying: ﴿And among mankind﴾, that is, the wavering and vacillating, ﴿who﴾ does not strive to elevate and refine his soul, so he denies and is destroyed by his evil deeds, because he ﴿disputes about God﴾, that is, about the power of the Supreme King over that Day and over other matters of His, after knowledge of them had reached him, out of audacity against His mighty authority, ﴿without knowledge﴾, but rather by falsehood, which is pure ignorance, so he abandons following the guiding, sincere advisers, ﴿and follows﴾ with utmost effort in his disputing ﴿every devil﴾, that is, one burning with evil, removed far away by the curse.

Since the context is to dispraise his follower, he indicated that he has no aim in following him except evil. There is no ambiguity in his matter, so the intensive form (*ṣīghat al-mubālaghah*) was not used, as passed in Sūrat al-Nisāʾ and as comes in Sūrat al-Ṣāffāt. So He said: ﴿rebellious﴾ (*marīd*), that is, stripped bare for corruption, with no occupation other than it, so he is in utmost ferocity against it. Al-Bayḍāwī said: its origin is *al-ʿurā*, meaning bare, empty ground.

﴿Was decreed﴾, that is, it was judged and ordained as an inescapable certainty that cannot be avoided. This is an expression by the necessary consequence (al-lāzim) for that which it necessitates (al-malzūm).

﴿for him﴾, that is, for that Satan, ﴿that whoever takes him as an ally﴾ (p-٨), that is, does toward him what an ally does toward his ally, by following him and turning to what he adorns, ﴿he will indeed mislead him﴾ by means of what makes the obedient acts hateful to him, so that he strays from the path of good.

Since the verse has discouraged taking him as an ally by pointing out that he misleads, and since misguidance is disliked by everyone, it clarifies that this is misguidance with no guidance in it at all. So it says: ﴿and guides him﴾, that is, by means of the desires that he makes attractive to him, which lead to slips. This is to inform that if he does lead him to anything, it is ﴿to the punishment of the Blaze﴾.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 22, verse 5:

When He had warned people about that Day, and had informed them that some of them deny it, and had made known its outcome, which implies that some of them affirm it and so their condition is the opposite of that of the deniers, and since many of those who affirm it act as the deniers act, He, glorified is He, turned to them a second time in mercy, alerting them that there should be no kind of doubt in their hearts about that Day, because of the signs in the horizons and in themselves that point to it. So He said, indicating it by both matters: ﴿O mankind﴾, that is, all of them. It is also possible that only the deniers are meant. He used "mankind" (al-nas), which is among the lowest of the descriptions, for this purpose, and as an indication that the deniers, and those who act in accordance with denial even if they affirm it, are the majority of mankind. He expressed it with the particle of doubt ﴿if﴾ as an indication that what the situation requires is their certainty about it. He made the condition past, and made clear that he used it only for rebuke, not because of doubt about their affair. By "was" (kāna) and the adverbial phrase he indicated how doubt had taken hold of them, so He said: ﴿you are in doubt﴾, that is, in uncertainty, suspicion, and need of clarification, ﴿concerning the resurrection﴾, which is the standing of bodies with their souls as they were before their death, the same as before, in order to magnify the idea that We could have power over it. ﴿Indeed We created you﴾ by Our power, which nothing can overwhelm, ﴿from dust﴾ that had never previously had the attribute of life, ﴿then from a drop of semen﴾, whose state is the furthest thing from the state of dust, for it is white, flowing, viscous and pure, as He said: ﴿from a gushing fluid﴾ [al-Tariq: 6]. Its origin is a little water, as al-Baghawi said. The origin of the word nutfah is pouring, as al-Baydawi said.

﴿Then from a clinging clot﴾, that is, a piece of red, solid blood that has no capacity to flow. ﴿Then from a lump of flesh﴾, that is, a very small piece of flesh into which the drop developed, ﴿formed﴾ with the complete form of a human being, ﴿and unformed﴾. That is, We created you from dust, which is of this nature, and We move it through these stages until it becomes a lump of flesh. Sometimes We shape it, and it becomes a human being; sometimes We do not shape it, but expel it from the womb corrupted, or its heat burns it, or it is not fully shaped but incomplete while the soul is present, like the one who was split (shiqq), who was a human half, and the sațīḥ, who was all upper body without a lower part, and similar cases. ﴿So that We may make clear to you﴾ the perfection of Our power and the completeness of Our wisdom, and that this is not something arising from nature, for if it arose from nature it would not vary. Its variation therefore shows that it comes from a chooser, a powerful and dominating agent. The object is omitted to indicate that it includes everything that minds can encompass.

Since the implicit sense was: We cause to miscarry from it what We do not will to complete, He followed it with His words: ﴿and We settle in the wombs﴾, that is, from that which We created, ﴿what We will﴾ to complete, ﴿for an appointed term﴾ that We determined for its completion, between six months and whatever more We wish beyond that, according to the strength and weakness of the wombs, the strength and weakness of what is formed, the abundance and scarcity of the blood it feeds upon, its purity and impurity, and other conditions and affairs that none knows but its Creator, whose power is exalted and whose greatness is high. As for what We do not will to complete, the wombs expel it by Our power, casting it out before completion, or burn it so that it perishes. ﴿Then We bring you forth﴾ after that ﴿as infants﴾, that is, in the state of childhood, small of body and weak in frame, hearing, sight and all the senses, ﴿so that you may not destroy your mothers by the largeness of your bodies and the greatness of your frames. The word (ṭifl) applies to the plural, and He used it instead of the plural form because of the equality in weakness of the outward and inward aspects.

When He mentioned the weakest weakness, He mentioned the greatest strength, joining it to what came before with a particle of sequence, because of the interval between them: ﴿then﴾, that is, We prolong your term ﴿so that you may reach﴾ by moving through the ages of bodies, between suckling, to the state of youth, to the time of puberty, the strength of youth and full maturity, ﴿your full strength﴾, that is, the end of every strength We determined for each of you. ﴿And among you is one who is taken﴾ before what comes after that of the age of old age. ﴿And among you is one who is returned﴾ to old age. He made the verb passive to indicate how easy it is for Him, even though it seems strange, were it not for the repeated observation of onlookers of such strength, vigour, and good connection among the limbs and their joining, ﴿to the lowest age﴾, which is the age of senility, when all its powers diminish, ﴿so that he will not know﴾

Since the context concerns the power to resurrect, which is the transformation from the state of inanimacy to its opposite with the utmost speed, He used the initial "min" (from) to indicate how close the time of ignorance is to the time of knowledge. Often a person spends the night in the fullest recollection of what he knows and mastery of it, then in the morning, or after a very short number of days without much gradual decline, knows nothing. The omission of the particle of termination indicates that his knowledge may return to him, and his ignorance may remain until death, unlike what came before in Surat al-Nahl. So He said: ﴿after knowledge﴾ that he had been given, ﴿anything﴾. Rather, he becomes as he was as a child in weakness of substances and accidents, so that you may know that all of that is the act of the one God, the chooser, and that if it were the act of nature, it would have increased in growth in all of that through prolonged survival. It is known with certainty, from the return of a human being to the loss of knowledge and small body to something like (p-12) what he was at the beginning of creation, that the One who returned him to that is certainly able to return him after death, and to the state of dust and decay.

When this proof concerning the Hour was complete, its premises sound and its conclusions clear, and since the first act of origination in it was not observed, He expressed it in a fitting way. He followed it with another proof that is perceptible, and joined it to what the implied sense points to, such as His words: "You, O people, find what We have mentioned in yourselves." So He said: ﴿And you see﴾, expressing it by sight, ﴿the earth﴾. Since it is in the context of resurrection, He expressed it with what is closer to death, saying: ﴿lifeless﴾, that is, dry, still, quiet, with the stillness of the dead, with nothing of vegetation in it. Perhaps He used the singular pronoun to address everyone who can be addressed by this. ﴿And when﴾, that is, We send down upon it water from a place where none is found, and it descends from there only by immense power and overwhelming dominion. Then when ﴿We send down upon it water﴾ with what We possess of greatness, ﴿it stirs﴾, that is, it moves with the sprouting of plants, shaking as a living thing does, and becomes ready to bring them forth. Al-Razi said: al-ihtizāz is the intensity of movement in different directions.

﴿And it swells﴾, that is, it rises, and this is the first thing visible from it to the eye, and it increases and grows by what emerges from it of plants arising from dust and water. ﴿And it produces﴾ by Our decree ﴿of every lovely pair﴾, that is, every kind We paired with another kind, making the benefit of each complete through the other, ﴿beautiful﴾, that is, delightful, from among the various kinds of plants, varied in their colours, tastes, scents, forms, benefits and quantities, pleasing to the sight, fitting for eyes and insight. Al-Razi said: just as a plant moves from deficiency to completion, so the human being ascends from deficiency to completion. In the afterlife he reaches the completion prepared for him, of enduring life, wealth, knowledge, purity and eternity. That is, the happy one among them is in the abode of peace, free from the accidents of this world. End.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 22, verse 6:

When He, glory be to Him, had established these two proofs, He arranged upon them what is sought and the conclusion, saying by way of causal explanation: ﴿That﴾, i.e., what has preceded of the command to piety, and the warning from the majesty of God through the gathering (on the Day of Resurrection), and the inference drawn to it from His disposing of the development of man and plants into what contains within it kinds of wisdom and varieties of subtleties, ﴿is because﴾, i.e., by reason of your knowing that ﴿God﴾, i.e., the One comprising the attributes of perfection, ﴿He is﴾, i.e., alone, ﴿the Truth﴾, i.e., the One who is established in the most perfect establishment, such that this requires that He is able to do whatever He wills, for there is no permanence with incapacity. ﴿And that He gives life to the dead﴾, i.e., He is able to do so, since He is, as will come, ﴿the Most High, the Great﴾ (p-14). ﴿And that He is over everything﴾ of creation and other than it ﴿Powerful﴾. ﴿Indeed, His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [Yasin: 82].

{And} the Hour, about which warning has already been given, which is the time of the gathering of all creatures, "is coming, there is no doubt about it" in any respect, because of what points to it of things that cannot be denied, by the word of One whose word cannot be turned back, and He is Wise, so He does not break His promise, and it is not fitting in any way that He leave His servants without reckoning. "And that Allah" (by virtue of His majesty and wisdom) "will raise up" by giving life "those who are in the graves," for their presence and for judging between them there in everything about which they differed, because that is part of the justice which He has commanded, and by it many of His attributes appear in the most complete manner. The summary is that the meaning is: He, glory be to Him, said what has preceded and did what He mentioned of creating man and plants in these stages, so that it may be known that He is able over these matters and over everything.

And among the people (are those who, before this clarification, had held back from faith, and whoever believes upon hearing these decisive proofs), and among the people (those whose nature has become extremely dense) is one who disputes, with the utmost of his effort, concerning Allah, that is, concerning His power and what this noble Name comprises of His attributes after this clarification, which has no equal and no obscurity. (p-15) without knowledge: that which came to him from Allah through the tongue of one of His chosen servants, whether it is a Book or something else; nor guidance: that which led him by his intellect, whether by necessity or by inference; nor an illuminating Book: one that was established for him as coming from Allah. It is known that when these three are absent, his disputing is nothing but falsehood.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 22, verse 9:

﴿Thāniya ʿiṭfih﴾ means: at ease in his mind, turning away, arrogant, twisting his neck in that manner, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And when Our verses are recited to him, he turns away arrogantly﴾ [Luqman: 7]. Al-ʿiṭf (the side, and the place of inclination) originally means the side, and the place of inclination.

Since the context indicates that he is the most dense of the categories in nature, he expressed his intention with His saying: ﴿to mislead﴾, meaning others, ﴿from the path of Allah﴾, to make this understood, because a sensible person does not intend this. So the first category is a misguided follower, and this one is a caller for the people of misguidance. This is according to the reading with a ḍammah (liyuḍilla) of the majority (al-Jumhur). According to the reading with a fatḥah (liyaḍilla) of Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr, and Ruways from Yaʿqub, with a difference of transmission from him, the meaning is "who went astray," and it is of the type of tahakkum (mocking irony), as has been mentioned more than once: that is, he is so clever that it does not escape him that this is misguidance, so he reached it only by his own intention.

When He mentioned his action and its fruit, He mentioned what was prepared for him because of it, so He said: ﴿For him in this world is disgrace﴾, meaning humiliation and abasement, even if the time of his being given respite and his being blessed with comfort is long. ("It is a right upon Allah that He does not raise anything of this world except that He lowers it.") ﴿And We will make him taste﴾, meaning by what belongs to Us of majesty, ﴿on the Day of Resurrection﴾, the Day on which He gathers the creation by resurrection after death, ﴿the punishment of the Burning﴾, meaning by making him feel the pain of the punishment of the fire, as one who tastes feels a thing, just as he burned the hearts of the guided ones through his disputation in falsehood. It is said literally or figuratively.

ذَلِكَ (That) — i.e., the great punishment — بِما (because of what) — i.e., because of the cause of what ﴿قَدَّمَتْ يَداكَ﴾ ("your hands have sent forward") — i.e., by your deeds. However, it is the custom of the Arabs to attribute deeds to the hand, since it is the instrument of most work, and attributing to the hand what leads to it is more emphatic (أنكأ). وأنَّ (and because) — i.e., and because of the fact that اللَّهَ (Allah) — i.e., He to whom all perfection belongs — لَيْسَ بِظَلامٍ (is not one who wrongs) — i.e., not one who does any wrong لِلْعَبِيدِ (to the servants). Had He left you otherwise, it would have been, in the course of your customary dealings, an injustice: first, by equating the doer of good with the doer of evil; and second, by leaving aside the support of those who were hostile to you in it and their harm on account of it. It is also permissible that the form (صيغة) is intensive (للمبالغة) so as to convey that if He had left it, injustice would have occurred, and that is in the utmost remoteness from His wisdom. . . He negated the very root of injustice from His manifest signs.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 22, verse 11:

When he had explained the two categories of those who openly profess disbelief, the thick and the thicker, and had made the sincere believer understood, he linked to that the wavering one, saying: ﴿And among the people is one who worships Allah on an edge﴾. For this reason he expressed it with "the people" (al-nas), whose implication is instability and hesitation, rather than saying "whoever worships Allah" (man ya'budu Allah), meaning one who acts in a manner of continuity and renewal by what the Supreme God has commanded, in obedience to Him, ﴿on an edge﴾. He is therefore unsteady, like the unsteadiness of one who stands on the brink of a precipice or a mountain or the like, with no stability for him. He is like one who is on the edge of an army: if he sees booty, he settles; if he imagines fear, he flies off and flees. That is the meaning of His saying: ﴿If good befalls him﴾, that is, of the worldly kind, ﴿he is reassured by it﴾, that is, by its cause, and remains upon what he is upon. ﴿But if a trial befalls him﴾, that is, a calamity, and if you say, by what the feminine form indicates, a trial, in his body or his livelihood, by which he is tested and his hidden state is shown to the people, ﴿he turns back upon his face﴾, because he is prepared to turn about, by being on the brink of a precipice, so he falls from that edge of religion into a fall after which there is no return to it and no movement with it. For a person is naturally disposed to ward off with every limb of his body anything coming at his face, so he does not yield to it except after the utmost of helplessness. The meaning is that he returns to the state in which he was, of disbelief or doubt, a return firmly established. This is in contrast to one firmly rooted in his faith: if prosperity befalls him, he gives thanks, and if adversity befalls him, he praises God and is patient; for every decree of Allah is good for him.

Since this turning back corrupts his hereafter by the burden he has incurred, and is of no benefit to him in making up what he has lost of the world, the conclusion of this is His saying: (p-١٨) ﴿He has lost the world﴾, that is, because this does not restore what has escaped him of it, and it becomes the cause of straitening upon him and the loss of its blessing, ﴿and the Hereafter﴾, by the forfeiture of the reward of patience and the incurring of the sin of impatience. Then He magnified his calamity by saying: ﴿That is﴾, that is, the great matter, ﴿it is﴾, that is, nothing else, ﴿the manifest loss﴾. Al-Bukhari related in the Tafsir from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, regarding this verse, that he said: A man would come to Medina, and if his wife bore a boy and his mares foaled, he would say, "This is a good religion," and if his wife did not bear and his mares did not foal, he would say, "This is a bad religion."

Then he explained this loss, which returned him to his state before the "edge" faith (al-īmān al-ḥarfī, a wavering faith held only at the margin), by his saying: ﴿he invokes﴾. That is, he worships, in reality or figuratively, with renewal and continuance, relying on other than Allah and rejecting ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾ [al-Fatiha: 5]. Since everything other than Allah is beneath Him, he drew attention to this by his saying: ﴿instead of Allah﴾. That is, [it is worship directed to something] of the lowest rank among the ranks of the one who combines the attributes of perfection.

Since what calls for worship is only action by choice, and what is driven by nature and compulsion has no weight in this matter, because one has no power to escape it and so the doer deserves no praise, he drew attention to this by his saying: ﴿that which does not harm him﴾. That is, in no way at all, not even by cutting off a benefit, if that could be imagined from it.

Since he placed harm first, because it is among the acceptable excuses for committing error, he followed it with benefit, to cut off every claim, and so he said: ﴿and that which does not benefit him﴾ in any way at all, nor by leaving off harm if it were to occur from it. Had the word "mā" been dropped from the second, one would think that blame requires the absence of both harm and benefit together, so that whoever claimed that one of them was absent from it would not be blamed. ﴿That﴾, that is, the act that indicates the greatest folly, which is invoking something that lacks the power to benefit, or something that lacks the power to harm, ﴿is﴾, that is, by itself, ﴿the far-gone error﴾, far from the truth and right guidance, which leads to deserts of confusion from which return is not possible. This is because the first, if one abandoned his worship, could not prevent his beneficence, and the second, even if one followed him, would not reach his benefit, nor would leaving off his harm. So worshipping them both is vain, because the doing of it and the leaving of it are equal.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 22, verse 13:

Since goodness naturally attracts a person, regardless of its source, because hearts are created to love those who do good to them, he (al-Biqa'i) clarified that what was said regarding the side of benefit is only by way of supposition, so He said: ﴿He calls﴾. Since what was first supposed, expressed by "mā" (what), may be non-rational, and so what proceeds from it would be due to its lacking reason (p-20), he removed this ambiguity by saying: ﴿to one whose harm is closer than his benefit﴾, that is, claiming that the one whose harm, even through his worship which brings the greatest misery, is closer than the benefit expected from him, is a god.

Since complete guardianship (wilāyah) befits only one from whom benefit is expected and harm is equally possible, because of his power over each of them by his own choice, and since the close companion (ʿashīr) is only suitable if his outcome is trustworthy, and since this one being called upon, if considered on the side of harm, is found unable to cause it, or on the side of benefit, is likewise, and even if the expectation of his benefit or harm is supposed, the fear of his harm is closer than the hope of his benefit, he deserves the utmost blame. For this reason, the Exalted began a new description of him by saying, expressing his blame with the particle placed for the totality of blame: ﴿Evil is the protector﴾, because he is not one whose benefit is hoped for, as he is one whose harm is feared, ﴿and evil is the companion﴾, because he is not one whose harm is safe, so he is unfit for guardianship or companionship in any way.

When he had made clear what preceded, that this god who is called upon is able to bring about both benefit and harm by way of testing, and that the possibility of either occurring from Him is equal, he drew attention to this by saying, beginning a new sentence (mustaʾnafan): ﴿Indeed, Allah﴾, that is, the one possessing all the attributes of perfection, exalted above every trace of imperfection, ﴿admits those who believe﴾ in His messengers and in what they called to concerning His affair, ﴿and do﴾ righteous deeds in confirmation of their faith, ﴿the good deeds﴾ that are pure, (p-٢١) bearing witness to their steadfastness in faith after harm had come upon them in this world through various kinds of afflictions, purifying them of the slips they had committed and the lapses that had led them astray, ﴿into gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾, that is, from whatever place of its land you wish, ﴿the rivers﴾. Since this was a remarkable matter, he indicated its ease by saying, explicitly stating what the context had conveyed from the description of choice: ﴿Indeed, Allah﴾, that is, the one encompassing everything in power and knowledge, ﴿does what He wills﴾ of every benefit and harm.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 22, verse 15:

When he had completed the proof concerning the loss of this one who turns back on his face and the gain of the one who stands firm, and this implied that whoever hopes for what God has promised rushes to turn to Him and benefits only himself, while whoever does not hope for that turns away from God, glorified is He, turning back on his face, and so harms only himself, he expressed the state of this second one, the worshipper "on an edge" (ʿalā ḥarf), with his words: ﴿Whoever thinks﴾, meaning, of those who have been struck by a trial, ﴿that God will not help him﴾, the Possessor of Majesty and Honour, in any of his circumstances, ﴿in this world and the Hereafter﴾. So he turns away from Him, turning back on his face, for he harms only himself, even if he thinks that he does not harm it. ﴿Then let him stretch out a rope﴾, meaning a cord or some other means that connects him ﴿to the sky﴾, which he wishes to reach, whether a ceiling, a cloud, or something else.

Since stretching that out is difficult or impossible for him, he expressed what follows from it with the particle of delay (al-ḥarf al-tarākhī, the particle of delay) and said: ﴿Then let him cut off﴾, meaning, let him make a connection and a severance from it, that is, let him exert his effort to repel the decree and destiny from himself. It is a command particle (lām al-amr) according to the one who vocalizes it with a kasra, to convey the intensity of the motion in the exertion toward descending to the lowest point, which indicates lack of reason; these are Abū ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir, Warsh from Nāfiʿ, and Ruways from Yaʿqūb. Or he makes it quiescent, as do the rest. ﴿Then let him look﴾ with his sight and his insight ﴿whether his scheming will remove﴾, however hard he strives, ﴿that which enrages him﴾, meaning, something from which he gets rage. Or the meaning is: let him do what one does who has been overcome by rage, by tying a rope to the ceiling of his house, then tying it around his neck, then cutting off what is between his feet and the ground so that he chokes. This is like saying to one whose affair has turned away from him and who grows distressed: "Strike your head against the wall if you are not content with this, die of rage," and the like. The summary is that if he does not endure afflictions for God willingly, he will endure them unwillingly, along with what he has gained of the causes of misery.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 22, verse 16:

When Glorified is He had made clear these visible signs, in these lofty methods, with this healing and guiding clarification by the miraculous nature of His judgment, He made clear that it is also miraculous in its composition (nazm). So He said: ﴿And thus﴾, that is, and in the same manner as We have made clear these visible signs, We have sent down Our speech for the clarification of its rulings and the manifestation of its secrets, ﴿We have sent it down﴾, that is, the whole speech, with the dazzling greatness that is Ours (p-23) ﴿as clear signs﴾, its composition being miraculous, just as its judgment is miraculous.

Since the discourse had made it clear that the implied meaning is: so that whoever goes astray, despite this clarification, may know that Allah leads astray whomever He wills, He followed it with His saying: ﴿And that﴾, that is, and so that he may know that ﴿Allah﴾, that is, the One described with generosity as He is described with retribution, ﴿guides﴾, that is, by His signs, ﴿whomever He wills﴾, that is, to make manifest His power and His choice, as a relief to the distress of one who says: If the visible and audible signs are of this degree of clarity, then why do most people, in their misguidance, have causes that fail to produce their effects?

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 22, verse 17:

When that was necessitating a question about the condition of the two groups, the guided and the astray, He answered that by explaining all the sects of error, because this surah has the most complete view of the Day of Gathering, which is the aim of the surah before it. So He intended to encompass the sects, depicting that Day in the most fitting image, and He paired each of the two groups of the People of the Book with a counterpart in meaning. He said: ﴿Indeed, those who believed﴾, meaning from whatever sect they were, and He expressed it with the verb so as to include affirmation by the tongue, which is the least of the aspects of faith. ﴿And those who became Jews﴾, meaning those who adopted Judaism, in whatever state they were, whether of faith or disbelief.

Since the Jews worshipped idols, seeking nearness through them to the stars (p-24), as has passed in al-Ma'idah, He followed them with those who resembled them, and said: ﴿and the Sabians﴾. Then He turned to the second of the two groups of the People of the Book and said: ﴿and the Christians﴾. Then He followed them with those who resembled them in part of their sects in their saying of two gods, and said: ﴿and the Magians﴾, who are the fire-worshippers. Then He concluded with the most general of all in error, just as He opened with the most general of them in guidance, and said: ﴿and those who associated partners﴾, because it includes every kind of association, even the minor kind such as riba and other things. ﴿Indeed, Allah﴾, meaning the Supreme King to whom all sovereignty belongs, and He is the most Judicious of judges, ﴿will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection﴾, so He will recompense each according to his deed in accordance with what it requires within the course of your customs, and will exact retribution for some of them from others, and will distinguish the wicked among them from the good. Then He gave the reason for that by His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah﴾, meaning the One gathering all the attributes of perfection, ﴿over all things﴾, of all things whatsoever, ﴿is Witness﴾. Nothing is except that He knows it, and therefore He is over all things capable, as its explanation has passed in ﴿He has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾ [Ta-Ha: 98] in Ta-Ha. Al-Harali said in explaining the Beautiful Names: witnessing is the seeing of experiential knowledge of the inner reality and essence of a thing, by one who has sufficiency in his matter. There is no witnessing except with experiential knowledge and sufficiency, by one who has balance within himself, so that he does not wrong others, and thus he is a scale of justice between himself and others, and it befits him to be a scale between every two disputants whose matter he encompasses in knowledge. ﴿And thus We made you a justly balanced nation that you may be witnesses over the people and the Messenger may be a witness over you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143]. And in proportion to the comprehensiveness of the witness's knowledge (p-25) is his testimony feared, and for this reason the most awe-inspiring testimony is the testimony of Allah over His creation: ﴿Say, "What thing is greatest in testimony?" Say, "Allah"﴾ [al-An'am: 19]. And since comprehensiveness, experiential knowledge, and watchfulness belong to Allah in the fullest sense, in reality there is no witness except Him. - End.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 22, verse 18:

Since everything previously mentioned in this surah indicates that He is capable of everything and that He does what He wills, and since He concluded this by stating that He has knowledge of everything, nothing is absent from Him and nothing escapes Him, this required His self-subsistence (qayyumiyya), and it is something that is considered great because of the multitude of creatures, so how much more so their conditions. He established this in answer to one who seems to have asked, so it carries the sense of a cause (or reason). He said: ﴿Do you not see that Allah﴾, that is, the One who possesses all perfection, free of every deficiency, ﴿prostrates to Him﴾, that is, submits, obeying His command, subjected to what He wills from them, subjugated like one who is at the utmost exertion in worship and sincerity in it, ﴿whoever is in the heavens﴾.

Since the context requires emphasis on the attribute of self-subsistence through testimony, and it mentioned the separation among all the groups, he emphasized it by repeating the relative pronoun, and said: ﴿and whoever is on the earth﴾. If it excludes non-rational beings, then it is by way of predominance (taghlib, the masculine rational gender prevailing over the non-rational); and if it is specified, then by the rational, it conveys that the submission of others is by way of a fortiori (min bab al-awla). Since he mentioned what includes the rational and the non-rational, he followed it with the most noble of what he mentioned of the non-rational, because each of them has been worshipped besides Allah, or some part of them has been worshipped. So he said: ﴿and the sun and the moon and the stars﴾, from the celestial bodies. The Himyar worshipped the sun, Kinana the moon, Tamim al-Dabaran, Lakhm al-Shi'ra, Tayyi' al-Thurayya, Asad Utarid, and Rabi'a al-Mirzam; this was said by Abu Hayyan. Then he followed that with the notable earthly entities, so he said: ﴿and the mountains﴾, that is, from which idols are hewn, ﴿and the trees﴾, some of which have been worshipped, ﴿and the moving creatures﴾, from which cattle have been worshipped. All these things submit to the command of Allah, and it is known, since these do not reason, that His command to them is His will concerning them.

Since the responsible rational beings have entered into His saying ﴿and whoever is on the earth﴾ as a primary entry, and since the prostration that is praised is only that which conforms to the command, not merely that which conforms to the bare will free of command, He said, indicating His will here by repeating them and dividing them after including them in the prostration of will and generalizing them: ﴿And many of mankind﴾, that is, prostrate in a prostration which is from him a legislated worship, so reward is due to him; ﴿and many﴾, that is, of them, ﴿have deserved the punishment﴾, because the proof has been established against them by their not prostrating. So he denied the command, and whoever denies it is a disbeliever, even if he is prostrating and worshipping in the linguistic sense, which is following (al-jary ma'a al-murad) what is willed. According to the view that this is in the estimation of a verb derived from the first word but with a meaning other than its own, it is close to what is called istikhdam (a device where a term is used in one sense and a pronoun refers to it in another), in which a pronoun refers to a word with one meaning while another meaning is intended by it. The verse is of ihtibak (a device of balanced omission): the affirmation of prostration in the first part is evidence for its negation in the second, and the mention of punishment in the second is evidence for the omission of reward in the first.

Since it is known from this that all are following the will and submitting in the most complete submission under the obedience of the decree, and that He made the command and prohibition for the responsible only as a means of making the fortunate among them happy and the wretched miserable, to establish the proof against them according to what they know of their conditions among themselves, the meaning is: whoever Allah honors by His success in complying with His command, then there is no one to humiliate him. He then joined to it: ﴿and whoever Allah humiliates﴾, that is, He to whom all command belongs, by rejecting His command, ﴿then there is none to honor him﴾, because there is no power for anyone else at all. Perhaps he mentioned this and omitted the first because the context is to manifest power, and manifesting it in humiliation is more complete, though the original context is for threat. Then he gave the reason that the action is His alone and not for another, by his saying: ﴿Indeed Allah﴾, that is, the Greatest King, ﴿does what He wills﴾, that is, all of it. So if it were permissible for another to prevent Him, even for a moment, He would not be doing what He wills. Thus it is established that there is no action for other than Him.

Ibn Kathir said: Ibn Abi Hatim said: Ahmad ibn Shayban al-Ramli narrated to us from al-Qaddah, from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that it was said to him: "Here there is a man who speaks about the will." So Ali said to him: "O servant of Allah, did Allah create you as He willed or as you willed?" He said: "Rather as He willed." He said: "Does He make you ill when He wills or when you will?" He said: "Rather when He wwills." He said: "Does He heal you when He wills or when you will?" He said: "Rather when He wills." He said: "Does He admit you where you will or where He wills?" He said: "Rather where He wills." He said: "By Allah, if you had said other than that, I would have struck the one in whom your two eyes are with the sword." What was mentioned in Surah Yusuf at the verse ﴿The judgment is only for Allah; upon Him I have relied﴾ [Yusuf: 67] is useful here.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 22, verse 19:

When He divided people into one who opposes and one who agrees, He followed this with their recompense, by that which encourages the one who agrees and frightens the one who opposes, in a manner that necessitates enjoining what is right (al-amr bi'l-ma'ruf), of which jihad is part, done sincerely for His sake alone. So He said: ﴿These two are opposing parties﴾, that is, the prostrating believer and the denying disbeliever from all the sects, ﴿who dispute﴾; complete reconciliation between them is not possible, since each of them is at one extreme.

When He indicated with the dual to each group among them, they became, despite their multitude and spread, through the unity of word in belief, like one body. He then made their multitude explicit by using the plural form, so He said: ﴿They dispute﴾, that is, they engaged in dispute with utmost effort. And since all the aforementioned groups affirm, and most of them have denied (p-29) the blessing, He said: ﴿concerning their Lord﴾, that is, the One to whose bounty toward them they confess. They did not dispute for any cause other than Him at all. Hamzah ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, the Lion of Allah and the Lion of His Messenger, and 'Ubaydah ibn al-Harith, and 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, who were the first to come forward for the contest in the presence of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, may Allah be pleased with them, against the disbelievers from among their paternal cousins: 'Utbah ibn Rabi'ah, Shaybah ibn Rabi'ah, and al-Walid ibn 'Utbah, at the Battle of Badr, are the most deserving of people of this verse, because of what is related in the Sahih from Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, that he used to swear that it was revealed concerning them. For this reason he, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "I am the first to kneel before the Most Merciful, Mighty and Majestic, on the Day of Resurrection, for the dispute." Al-Bukhari reported it in his Sahih. Perhaps he, may Allah be pleased with him, was the first of the three who rose to oppose them in opposition to the Prophet ﷺ, for he was more fervent in it.

When He mentioned their dispute and its condition, He mentioned their recompense for it in the decisive matter He had previously mentioned, and He began with the warning, because the human being is more in need of it. So He said: ﴿As for those who disbelieve﴾, opposing the command of their Lord, ﴿garments of fire will be cut out for them﴾, cut in a manner whose multitude none knows but Allah, with the easiest of matters from One whose command none else possesses. ﴿For them﴾ now, and it has been prepared, even though they agreed with His intention by opposing His command. ﴿Garments of fire﴾ will encompass them, and they will be fitted to their measures, enveloping them, just as they used to strip off garments in the world out of arrogance and haughtiness, while they are in a state in which ﴿there will be poured﴾ over their heads, when they enter it, ﴿boiling water﴾, that is, water of such intense heat that its degree is known only by tasting it. May Allah protect us from it.

Having resumed the report about it with His words: ﴿Whereby there shall be melted﴾, that is, dissolved (yudhābu). Its root meaning is intense mixing ﴿by it﴾ because of the intensity of its heat, ﴿what is in their bellies﴾ of fat and other things, ﴿and the skins﴾, so that its effect will be the same within and without.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 22, verse 21:

﴿And for them are maqāmi'** (maqami‘) — the plural of miqma‘ah, with a kasra then a fatha — which is an iron club with which the head and face are struck, so as to turn the one struck back from his purpose with a violent repulsion. Then he negated the metaphorical sense by his saying: ﴿of iron﴾, meaning: they will subdue them with them.﴾

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 22, verse 22:

﴿Whenever they wish﴾ i.e., all of them, so a portion (of them) is included a fortiori, ﴿to come out of it﴾ i.e., out of those garments or out of the Fire.

Since the context concerns the contention of the friends of Allah, who are characterized by what is the aim of the surah, namely taqwa (God-consciousness), against the disbelievers, who oppose it in every respect, this requires glad tidings for the friends and warning for the enemies. His statement, in addition to what is in the (previous) prostration verse: ﴿from distress﴾, a great distress whose magnitude none knows except Allah, ﴿they will be returned﴾, every one of those ﴿in it﴾, as if they were being struck by the blaze of the Fire, so that it lifts them until, when they are at its top, they are struck with iron hooks and they fall into it for seventy autumns. This is the statement of al-Hasan. Or, they will be thrashed about in those garments cut out of Fire, to the point that they nearly come apart from them while they are in the Fire, and then they are returned as they were, and this is more severe in punishment, (it being) said to them: ﴿Return humiliated﴾, enduring its distresses. ﴿And taste the punishment of the burning﴾, i.e., the punishment that reaches the extreme of burning.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 22, verse 23:

When he had mentioned what belongs to one of the two adversaries, namely the disbelievers, he followed it with what belongs to the other, namely the believers. He changed the style to emphasis for one who seemed to be asking about them, magnifying them by stating the proper name that comprises all attributes, as a notice of concern, so He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah﴾, i.e., the One to whom belongs all the command, ﴿will admit those who believed﴾. He expressed belief with the past tense, encouraging haste in bringing it about, ﴿and did righteous deeds﴾, as confirmation of their faith. He expressed it with the past tense to indicate that whoever does righteous deeds has the goodness that was hidden from him revealed, so he loves it and does not part from it. ﴿Gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾, i.e., constantly, ﴿beneath which rivers flow﴾, i.e., abundant waters; wherever you wish in its land, a river flows for you, in contrast to what flows above the heads of the people of the Fire. ﴿They will be adorned therein﴾, in contrast to what still comes from the inner and outer parts of the disbelievers, ﴿with bracelets﴾

Since the purpose of this surah is to urge piety, which leads to bestowal of grace, He made them desirous of it by the most precious adornment we know, so He said: ﴿of gold and pearls﴾. The reading of Nafi' and 'Asim with the accusative of it (لؤلؤا) is evidence that it is coordinated by the genitive with "bracelets" (أساور). ﴿And their clothing therein will be silk﴾, in contrast to the garments of the disbelievers, just as the clothing of the disbelievers in this world was silk, while the clothing of the believers was less than that. It is reported in the two Sahihs, from 'Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: "Do not wear silk, for whoever wears it in this world will not wear it in the Hereafter." Ibn Kathir said: 'Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr said, "And whoever does not wear silk in the Hereafter will not enter Paradise." Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And their clothing therein will be silk﴾. End of quotation. "That is because in the two Sahihs and others, from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, the Prophet, may Allah bless him, said: 'Only one who has no share in the Hereafter wears this,'" so it is near that Allah will join him to them, through his imitation of the disbelievers in their clothing, so that he does not die a Muslim. And Allah is the Guide.

Wa-hudu ("and they were guided"): that is, with the easiest matter, by the guidance of God, in a general sense, not limited to this intellect alone as the immediate cause, nor to the Messenger, nor to the Book, nor to anything else. It is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "those who believe." What follows it was concluded with it so that the separation between the verb and its object would not be prolonged, and so that their good qualities would encompass the mention of their entry into Paradise, as an indication of its permanence. ﴿Unto goodly speech﴾, so they remained in a good state. "And they were guided" — here the verb is also put in the passive form, indicating the ease of guidance for them and for the pious among them. For this reason, the (divine) might is not mentioned, and mention of praise is sufficient, so it says: ﴿to the path of the Praiseworthy﴾, who enabled them to follow that for which they are praised, (p-33) so they are praised in the outcome. Thus their action was good, just as their speech was good. So they entered Paradise, which is the most noble abode, in the presence of the best of neighbors, and they were adorned therein with the noblest of ornaments, just as they were adorned in this world with the noblest of ways. This is after they had attained the noblest mention in this world, in contrast to the state of the disbelievers in committing what caused them to enter (the Fire), that whenever they wished to leave it they were returned to it, along with the bad repute that befell them, by their turning toward the perishable like cattle, despite its baseness, because it is present, and their turning away from the lasting, despite its nobility, because it is absent.

When al-Biqa'i had explained the outcome for the two groups, and the description of the second group included an account of their deeds that indicate the truthfulness of their faith, he repeated mention of the first group to explain what indicates the continuation of their disbelief, and to confirm the explanation of their recompense. So He said: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾, meaning, they committed this wicked act. Since the present tense (al-mudari') may be used without a specific time in mind, whether present or future, and may intend only the sense of continuity, as in the saying of people, "So-and-so gives and withholds," He joined to the past tense the following: ﴿and bar﴾, meaning, and they persist in barring, ﴿from the way of Allah﴾, meaning the Supreme King, by their dividing among themselves the roads of Makkah. Some of them would say to whoever passed by them: "A sorcerer has come out among us," another says, "A poet," and another, "A soothsayer. Do not listen to him, for he wants to turn you away from your religion." One of those who embraced Islam said: "They did not cease with me until I put cotton wool (kursuf) in my ears, for fear that I would hear something of their speech." They used to harm those who embraced Islam, in addition to other of their deeds. Perhaps He expressed it with the present tense out of mercy toward them, so that it would function like a condition regarding disbelief, which indicates that whoever abandons barring, disbelief departs from him, even if that barring had lasted long. ( And ) they bar from "the Sacred Mosque" (al-Masjid al-Haram), that its rites be upheld, namely circumambulation of the House, prayer, Hajj and 'Umrah, by those who are its people, from among our friends. Then He described it with what shows the severity of their wrongdoing in barring from it, so He said: ﴿which We have made﴾, by the greatness We possess, ﴿for the people﴾, meaning all of them. Then He explained this making (of it) for them by His saying: ﴿equal for the one who dwells there﴾, meaning the resident, ﴿and the outsider﴾, meaning the one who comes to visit it from the desert. Al-Razi said in al-Lawami': ﴿equal﴾ is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), and ﴿the one who dwells﴾ is its predicate, and its indefiniteness is acceptable as a subject because it is like a generic noun in conveying generality, which is the best kind of definiteness.

When He mentioned the disbelievers and the evidence of their disbelief, in a way that calls them to reflection, and increased this appeal by omitting the predicate concerning them, and the end of the verse indicated that He would make them taste the painful punishment, He joined to it what turns one away from their description, so He said: ﴿And whoever intends therein﴾, meaning anything of the deeds of the disbelievers, such as the barring mentioned and other things, that is, there arises from him an intention toward something of that sort, ﴿with deviation﴾, meaning that this intention is accompanied and tainted by injustice, departing from commanding the good, and by inclination and crookedness. Since this occurs in the absolute sense of this meaning, he clarified the intended sense by His saying: ﴿with wrongdoing﴾, meaning in other than its proper place. As for the barring of the disbelievers from it, it is in truth, for they are impure, and it is not fitting for them to approach the sacred precincts; likewise the barring of the menstruating woman, the one in a state of major impurity (junub), and the treacherous. ﴿We shall make him taste﴾. Since the condition is a kind of deviation and not complete deviation, He expressed it by His saying (p-٣٥) ﴿of a painful punishment﴾. This statement indicates, regarding whoever intends something of what the disbelievers did, that the report concerning the disbelievers who perform what this recompense is ordered for, upon their intending it, is what I have determined.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 22, verse 26:

When he (Allah) had mentioned the two groups (the believers and the disbelievers) and the recompense of each, and concluded this with the mention of the House (the Ka'bah), He followed it with a reminder of the House and of the Hajj to it, because in it there is a reminder of the Resurrection, which impels one to taqwa (God-consciousness), which is the aim of the surah; and because of what it contains of coming as a delegation (wifadah) to Allah, with detachment from worldly possessions (al-muhit), humility before the Lord, and gathering at the sacred sites (al-masha'ir), standing in one place after another; and because of what it contains of urging the emulation (al-tasannun) of their greatest father, Ibrahim (peace be upon him). So He said, rebuking and reproaching those who associated others in its benefit: "It was founded upon tawhid from the first day," in conjunction with His saying at the beginning of the surah, ﴿Fear your Lord﴾ [al-Hajj: 1]. ﴿And when﴾, meaning: and remember when ﴿We settled﴾ by what We have of greatness, and since He, glorified is He, did not make it (the House) a dwelling by Himself, He restricted the verb from transitivity to its first object, so He said: ﴿for Ibrahim﴾, meaning: We assigned for him ﴿the place of the House﴾, that is, the Ka'bah, and We made it for him a mubaa'ah, that is, a dwelling to which one returns (yaboo'u ilayhi), that is, returns, because it, by what We deposit in it of subtleties, is worthy that whoever departs from it should return to it and yearn for it, and whoever is far from it should long for it, and that some of his descendants should attach themselves to it. (p-36) The mubaa'ah in the sense of the dwelling (al-manzil); and "bawwa'ahu iyyahu" and "bawwa'ahu lahu," meaning he lodged him. Ibn Sayyidah said in Tartib al-Muhkam: "It was said: I prepared it and enabled him therein."

What indicates that Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was the first builder of the House is what is in the Sahih: "On the authority of Abu Dharr (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: I said: O Messenger of Allah! Which mosque was placed first? He said: The Sacred Mosque. I said: Then which? He said: The Masjid al-Aqsa (Bayt al-Maqdis). I said: How long between them? He said: Forty years."

Since Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was a prophet, it was known that his prophethood was for the sake of worship, so the meaning was: We said to him: Settle your family here and frequent this place for worship. This He explained by His saying: ﴿that you do not associate anything with Me﴾, so He began with the foundation and head of worship, and He joined to the prohibition His saying: ﴿and purify My House﴾ from everything unbecoming to it of physical and moral filth, of polytheism and idols, and of circumambulating it naked, as the Arabs used to do, ﴿for those who circle it﴾.

Since the devotion (al-'ukuf) had already been mentioned, He did not need to repeat it, so He said: ﴿and those who stand﴾, meaning around it, glorifying Me as is done around My Throne, or in prayer; and because standing in devotion is closer to the aim of the surah.

﴿and those who bow﴾. Since each of circumambulation and standing is an act of worship in its own right, while bowing and prostration are not like that, He joined the one and followed with the other, because of the complete connection between them, since in prayer neither of them is separated from the other, so He said: ﴿the prostrating﴾, meaning those who pray the prayer of the people of Islam in its most perfect form. (p-37)

﴿Wa-adhdhin fi al-nas﴾ means: inform them and call out to them, ﴿bi-al-hajj﴾ (the pilgrimage), which is the intention to go to the House repeatedly, for the worship specific to the sacred sites that are prescribed. ﴿Ya'tūka﴾ means: they will come to your House, which you built for this purpose, answering your call by Our permission, listening, obedient, humble, and submissive, ﴿from every deep ravine of the earth﴾, just as they answer the caller from Us when he calls them with the like of that after death. ﴿Rijālan﴾ means: on foot. ﴿Wa-ʿalā kulli ḍāmir﴾ means: on every lean camel, emaciated from the length of the journey, because of the great distance and the severity of the hardship.

Since al-ḍāmir (the lean one) applies to both the male and the female of camels, and the female is the weaker of the two kinds, the judgment of coming described above applying to her is a judgment applying to the male, which is stronger, by way of a fortiori reasoning. So it is attributed to her pronoun, and he said, expressing it with what indicates renewal and continuity, describing the lean ones that the word ﴿kull﴾ (every) implies: ﴿ya'tīna﴾ (they will come), meaning the lean ones, ﴿min kulli fajj﴾ (from every fajj), meaning a wide path between two mountains, ﴿ʿamīq﴾ (deep), meaning far and low in relation to the height of its mountains. Abu Hayyan said: its origin is distance downward, end of quote. They come barefoot and naked, moving from one of the sacred sites of (p-38) the Hajj to another, and from one place of standing to another, gathered by the call, humbled by the majesty, fearful of the might, hoping for forgiveness. Then they disperse to their homelands and turn toward their dwellings, like those travelling to the places of standing at the Gathering, on the Day of Resurrection and Dispersal, dispersing to the two abodes of bliss and hellfire. So, O you who believe that Our friend Ibrahim, peace be upon him, called out for the Hajj, and it was answered by Our power as an honour to him, for whomever God wills to perform His Hajj, despite the distance of their regions and the remoteness of their lands, from those who existed in that time and from those who were in the loins of the nearer or more distant forefathers! Affirm that the caller from Us, by the blowing of the Trumpet, will be answered by everyone who was upon its surface, whom We preserved his body, or whom We let the earth tear apart until he became dust, and whatever is between that, because all is easy for Us.

The commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 22, verse 28:

Since man is inclined toward benefits and eager for good customs, He gave as the reason for the coming (to the sacred sites) that which encourages him, granting from His bounty what he intends regarding the matter of livelihood, saying: ﴿that they may witness﴾, that is, that they may be present in full attendance, ﴿benefits for them﴾, that is, not for the One worshipped, both religious and worldly. For just as He, glory be to Him, made those places effacers of sins and attractors of hearts, He made them bringers of benefits, flowing in the best of customs, safe from poverty and mending of breakage. And since benefits do not become good nor bear fruit except through piety, the motive toward piety was (mentioned) by the words of remembrance: ﴿and mention the name of Allah﴾, that is, the One who gathers all perfections, through takbir and other (formulas) at the slaughter and otherwise, as an announcement (p-39) that He is the intended aim which all other aims follow, because it was He who gathered them upon that fertile land and those dusty places, by His complete power and all-encompassing might, not the name of any idol, as the Jahiliyyah used to do, ﴿on known days﴾, that is, days known with knowledge that they are the first ten (days) of Dhu al-Hijjah, the name of which agrees with its named reality, not what they named it while its reality is other, according to what the Nasi' (intercalation) decreed. In this there is an indication that what is meant by it is abundance (of remembrance), since mere remembrance is recommended at every time. And in the expression "with knowledge" there is an indication of the obligation to exert full effort, after certainty that the month of Dhu al-Hijjah, in name and reality, is (established) in determining its beginning. As for the days of tashriq, since they were founded upon knowledge of the matter of the month which He commanded here, and this produced knowledge of the day of the feast, no need arose regarding them except for counting, and therefore He expressed them by it rather than by knowledge.

And since livestock are the most noble of their wealth, the Exalted said, encouraging them and warning them: ﴿over﴾, that is, blessing (Allah) by mentioning Him and praising Him for ﴿what He has provided them﴾, even though, had He willed, He could have destroyed it, ﴿of the beast﴾. And since the beast is indefinite in every four-footed creature on land and sea, He specified it by His saying: ﴿of livestock﴾, namely camels, cattle and sheep, with takbir upon seeing them, then again at their slaughter. In this is an exhortation to draw near (to Allah) through sacrificial animals and offerings. For this reason He turned to address them directly. The root of "lahum" (for them) revolves around obscurity, concealment, closure and lack of distinction, while the root of "na'am" (livestock) revolves around ease, comfort and tranquility.

(p-40) And since the Exalted mentioned worship and addressed Ibrahim, upon him be peace, in order to alert that, because of the greatness of the One worshipped, none perform it in its proper manner except the sincere, He turned to all the worshippers, giving permission in what would gladden them from the gift of enjoyment, as an alert to the blessing and an incitement to gratitude. So He said, explaining what is included in that from the slaughter: ﴿So eat from them﴾, that is, if you wish, when you offer them voluntarily, and do not refrain as the people of the Jahiliyyah did. Eating from what is offered voluntarily does not remove it from being a qurban in this tolerant monotheistic way, as a favor to its people and an honoring of its Prophet ﷺ. Eating from what is obligatory is not permitted for one upon whom it is obligated, for if he eats from it he has not fully discharged what was obligated upon him. ﴿And feed the miserable﴾, that is, the one whose need is severe, from ba'isa (to be wretched) like sami'a, when his condition becomes bad and he becomes poor. And he clarified that it is from this, not from ba'usa (to be fierce) like karuma, whose meaning is "to be intense in war," by His saying: ﴿the poor﴾.

Al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on Surah 22, verse 29:

He confirmed this exhortation and removed any doubt about it by returning to the first style in His saying: ﴿Then let them end their state of neglect﴾, meaning let them cut off and complete, on the Day of Sacrifice (Yawm al-Nahr), after the long duration of ihram, ﴿their state of neglect (tafath)﴾, meaning their disheveled condition, by bathing, trimming the nails and the moustache, shaving the pubic area, and the like. ﴿And let them fulfil their vows﴾, taking this as derived from completing the matter and being free of every obligation. ﴿And let them circumambulate (yattawwafu)﴾, so that this will be the last of their acts. He urged (them) to do it abundantly and to strive in it by using the form tafa''ala, and to sincerity through concealment, as far as possible, by idgham (assimilation). The lam, if kasra-vowelled, as is the reading of Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir and Warsh from Nafi', Qunbul from Ibn Kathir, and Ruways from Ya'qub in ﴿liyaqdu﴾, and the reading of Ibn Dhakwan from Ibn 'Amir alone in "liyuwaffu... wa liyatawwafu", may be a lam of purpose, coordinated with ﴿that they may witness﴾ [al-Hajj: 28]. Its coordination with the particle of delay indicates the length of the period, together with an indication of the exaltation of rank. It may also be a lam of command, as in the reading of the rest with sukun. His saying ﴿by the House﴾ means "around it", (the House being) the place of the Hijr. Whenever the circuit around it falls short of completion by even a small part, it is not valid, because it does not fulfil the designation of circumambulation. Therefore the ba' here has no connection with partition (tab'id). Describing it with His saying ﴿the Ancient﴾ is an indication of its deserving exaltation by its antiquity and by being freed from every evil.

Then he pointed to the magnification of the Hajj and its rites with his words: ﴿That﴾, i.e., the matter that is great, mighty, and grand, whose benefits are great in this world and the next: that. Since the implied sense was: whoever does it is made happy, and whoever violates any part of it is made wretched, he followed it with his words: ﴿And whoever magnifies﴾, i.e., with the utmost of his effort, ﴿the sacred ordinances of God﴾, i.e., of the One of majesty and honor, all of them, whether from this [matter] or from others, and they are the things He made sacred for him, so He urged him to do them or to abstain from them. ﴿Then it is﴾ (p-42), i.e., the magnification that drives him to carry out the command concerning them in the proper manner and to avoid what is forbidden, such as circumambulating naked and slaughtering in the name of other than God, ﴿better﴾ and existing ﴿for him with his Lord﴾, Who bestowed upon him everything he has of blessings, so that thanking Him became obligatory for him. For that indicates the piety of his heart, because magnifying them is among the piety of hearts, and magnifying them is [magnifying] the majesty of God, while violating them is evil for him with his Lord.

Since the implied sense was: certain things have been made unlawful for you to do, and certain things to leave undone, he followed it with his words, explaining that the state of ihram does not affect them as it affects hunting: ﴿And the cattle have been made lawful for you﴾, which are camels, cows, and sheep, all of them, ﴿except what is recited﴾, i.e., continuously, in a renewed manner, ﴿to you﴾, its prohibition: carrion, blood, and what has been dedicated to other than God. This is in contrast to the unbelievers, who fabricated against God by worshipping through the prohibition of the wasila, the bahira, the sa'iba, and the ham, and the permitting of carrion and blood.

Since this implied the permissibility of the sa'iba and what accompanies it, and the prohibition of what is slaughtered for the idols (anṣāb), and since the cause of all of that was the idols, he made his words a consequence of this: ﴿So shun﴾, i.e., with the utmost effort, following the example of the great father Abraham, peace be upon him, to whom the instruction of this kind had already been given when the House was made his dwelling place, ﴿the filth﴾, i.e., the impurity which by right should be shunned even without a command; then he specified and distinguished it with his words: ﴿of the idols﴾, i.e., the impurity which by right should be shunned even without a command, for when the cause is shunned, the effect is shunned.

Since all of that is of falsehood, he followed it with a prohibition against all falsehood, and increased its severity and gravity, since he placed it alongside shirk, as the Prophet ﷺ said, and so he said: ﴿And shun﴾, i.e., in every respect, ﴿the word of falsehood﴾, i.e., all of it, which is deviation from the proof, like shirk, which leads to attributing inability to God and to forbidding what God has not sent down any authority for, such as the sa'iba and what accompanies it, and to permitting carrion and the like of what the revealed proof has established as prohibited, just as ḥanaf means inclining toward the proof. For this reason he followed it with his words.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 22, verse 31:

﴿Turning away from all false things, devoted to Allah﴾, He who possesses all perfection, so there is no inclination in anything of His acts. Both (al-zur and al-hanif) share a general sense of inclination, yet they are such because the root of al-zur (falsehood, false inclination) revolves around strength and roughness (al-wu'ura), whereas al-hanaf (inclination to truth), as was explained in al-Baqara, revolves around softness and ease (al-suhula). Thus the one who is false (dhu al-zur) turns away from the proof because of its density, while the hanif turns toward the proof with the gentleness it possesses.

When this (inclination to tawhid) was made clear, He emphasized it with His saying: ﴿not associating anything with Him﴾, that is, not associating any part of partnership, but rather being sincere to Him in religion. This indicates the greatness and loftiness of tawhid, and the abhorrence and lowliness of shirk, through His saying, as a deterrent from it and as a continuation of what is implied in the sense: whoever obeys this, his moderation raises him to the Highest Companion: ﴿And whoever associates others with Allah﴾, that is, whoever ascribes any part of shirk ﴿to Allah﴾, that is, to Him who possesses all greatness, ﴿to anything among things at any time﴾ (p-44) ﴿it is as if he had fallen from the sky﴾, because of the height of the summit of tawhid he was on and the lowness of the abyss of shirk to which he descended.

Since the one who falls from this height is necessarily broken into pieces, either by the predatory birds or by striking the ground, He expressed this with His saying: ﴿so the birds snatch him away﴾, that is, in pieces among them, while he is still in the air before reaching the earth. ﴿Or the wind throws him﴾, that is, to where he finds nothing in the air to destroy him, ﴿into a far-off place﴾ of the earth, ﴿sahiq﴾, that is, distant in its lowness, so that he is torn apart upon arriving at the earth by the force of the fall and the violence of the impact, due to the distance of the place from which he fell and slipped. Thus the verse is of the type of al-ihtibak: the snatching of the birds, which implies tearing apart, first indicates the omission of tearing apart second; and the far-off place, which implies reaching the earth second, is evidence of the omission of its opposite first. Then he magnified what preceded of tawhid and what is caused by it with a demonstrative of distance.

﴿That﴾, that is, the great matter. Whoever observes it succeeds, and whoever deviates from it fails. Then he joined to it something more general than this implied term, saying: ﴿And whoever﴾.
